title: Garlic and Onion Rust (Puccinia allii, syn. P. asperulae-odoratae / P. mixta sensu auct.)
content: Garlic rust, caused by the autoecious, brachycyclic (uredinia/telia only - no pycnial/aecial stages) basidiomycete rust fungus Puccinia allii (commonly referenced as P. porri in older literature; synonyms include Uromyces allii, P. asperulae-odoratae; correctly classified to Pucciniaceae section Uromycesporium) is the most important biotic constraint to garlic (Allium sativum L.), leek (A. ampeloprasum var. porrum), and shallot (A. cepa var. aggregatum) production worldwide in cool, humid production regions. The disease is especially severe in the Pacific Northwest garlic-growing areas of Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia, the northeastern USA, northern Europe (United Kingdom, Netherlands, Germany, Poland, France), the highlands of Kenya and Ethiopia, Japan, Korea, and the cooler southern areas of South America (Chile, Argentina, southern Brazil). Yield and quality losses of 30-80% are common on susceptible garlic cultivars in years with cool, wet springs; even moderate rust epidemics reduce marketable bulb diameter by 20-40% due to premature foliar dieback before bulb maturity. Symptoms occur on leaves, pseudostems, scapes, and occasionally bulb outer scales. The diagnostic symptom is the presence of small, oval to slightly elongated, bright orange-yellow to cinnamon-brown, powdery uredinial pustules 0.5-2 mm in diameter that erupt through the host epidermis on both leaf surfaces. The uredinia are produced in linear rows oriented parallel to the long axis of the strap-shaped Allium leaf (a useful diagnostic feature separating garlic rust from random Botrytis or Stemphylium lesions) and each pustule is surrounded by a small chlorotic or necrotic yellow halo on susceptible cultivars. On resistant garlic clones, pustules abort before rupturing and appear as minute necrotic tan flecks (Type 0 or Type 1 hypersensitive resistant reaction). As the garlic leaf matures and senesces in early summer, the cinnamon-colored uredinial pustules are gradually converted to dark brown to black telial pustules containing two-celled, thick-walled, oblong-clavate teliospores (45-70 x 20-30 um; pedicellate, germ pore apical in upper cell, equatorial in lower cell, wall 3-5 um thick) that function as overwintering spores. Severe rust infection of the leaves and pseudostem causes rapid leaf senescence, collapse of the foliage 2-3 weeks before normal harvest, and reduced translocation of carbohydrates into the developing bulbs; the result is under-sized, soft bulbs that do not store well because of incomplete skin curing and secondary invasion of bulb neck tissues by Erwinia bacteria, Botrytis neck rot, and Aspergillus niger black mold. Puccinia allii is an autoecious rust, completing its entire life cycle on Allium hosts without an alternate host. It is brachycyclic: uredinia (repeating, dikaryotic) are followed directly by telia (dikaryotic, karyogamy, meiosis on germination) without pycnial or aecial stages. Teliospores germinate after a chilling requirement of 4-8 weeks at 0-8 C to produce a four-celled basidium bearing four basidiospores that re-infect young Allium leaves the following spring; however, in many moderate-climate areas, the repeating uredinial stage also survives the winter on infected volunteer garlic, leek, and perennial Allium weed hosts (Allium triquetrum, A. vineale, A. canadense, A. oleraceum, A. ursinum, A. neapolitanum) and provides the initial spring inoculum directly without requiring sexual teliospore germination. Urediniospores are wind-dispersed for up to hundreds of kilometers under turbulent atmospheric conditions, but typical field-to-field spread is via rain splash, farm equipment, and workers' clothing on a local scale. Infection occurs through stomata after a required 4-10 hours of leaf wetness at temperatures of 10-22 C (50-72 F); infection rate drops sharply above 25 C, which explains why garlic rust is a problem only in cool spring growing conditions rather than hot dry summers. Management: (1) plant only rust-free certified seed garlic cloves from low rust-pressure seed-increase zones; do not save seed cloves from a rust-affected crop; select planting stock from a previous season with no visible uredinia or telia. (2) long, 3-4 year crop rotations with non-Allium crops, separated from prior Allium fields by at least 500 m to reduce airborne urediniospore drift where practical. (3) eliminate Allium weed reservoirs (wild garlic A. vineale, wild onion A. canadense, three-cornered leek A. triquetrum, ramsons A. ursinum, onionweed Nothoscordum borbonicum) from field borders, irrigation canals, and fence rows; rogue volunteer garlic and onion plants in the autumn and spring. (4) cultural: avoid excessively early fall plantings that produce large foliar canopies before winter dormancy; use moderate planting densities (20-30 cloves per m^2); do not apply excessive nitrogen (more than 150 kg N/ha) which promotes lush, highly susceptible tissue; use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers; orient rows north-south to maximize canopy solar exposure and leaf drying. (5) genetic resistance is the most effective long-term control strategy. The garlic cultivar collections maintained at USDA-ARS (1,200+ Plant Introduction accessions), INRA France, IPK Gatersleben Germany, and the Volcani Center Israel contain a broad range of rust reactions. Several P. allii major R genes have been characterized (Rga1, Rga2, Rga3 derived from A. sativum var. ophioscorodon Svalovs Jaune, A. tuncelianum, A. nigrum, A. longicuspis); the most popular US cultivars with moderate to high partial resistance are German White, Georgian Crystal, Persian Star, Killarney Red, Spanish Roja, and Rosewood. (6) fungicide programs in high-risk areas: begin protectant sprays at first detection of uredinia in spring and repeat on 10-14 day intervals through bulb maturity (at least 4 applications usually required). The most effective fungicide groups against garlic rust in Cornell and WSU OSU trials are FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (tebuconazole, tetraconazole, difenoconazole, myclobutanil, prothioconazole, metconazole, epoxiconazole - the DMI triazoles are the gold standard for rust on Allium crops because they provide both protectant and curative kickback activity of up to 96 hours post-infection), FRAC 11 QoI (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin - protectant only, do not use solo to prevent development of QoI-resistant P. allii populations reported already in UK and Oregon), FRAC 7 SDHI + FRAC 11 premixes (fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin, bixafen + prothioconazole, benzovindiflupyr + prothioconazole), FRAC U8 fluazinam, and multi-site FRAC M2 sulphur (dusting sulfur, micronized wettable sulfur) is an inexpensive protectant partner for DMI/QoI/SDHI resistance management as well as a principal control in organic production. Organic garlic rust programs use sulphur every 7 days in spring combined with potassium bicarbonate, plant extracts (Salix, Reynoutria sachalinensis), and Bacillus subtilis during dry periods and can reduce losses to 10-20% compared to unsprayed controls.
